summary: Every section is present but none says anything specific: no real user, no evidence for the problem, and nine features aimed at all knowledge workers.

results.fix: Replace the problem statement with one user and one observed failure, e.g. 'Engineering managers at 50-200 person companies lose decisions made in weekly syncs; 6 of 8 we interviewed re-litigated a decision within a month.' Say why it happens.

results.evidence: The engineering team will determine the best architecture.
results.fix: It's short, but short and vague. Cut each section to the one decision it records and delete any sentence a reader can't act on.

results.evidence: leverages cutting-edge large language models to revolutionize how teams collaborate
results.fix: Add the calls only you can make: which of the nine features you'd cut first and why, and what you learned that a competitor hasn't.
Write the problem, cause and intent yourself in five plain sentences, then use AI only to tighten and check them.

results.evidence: There is a significant opportunity to improve the meeting experience with AI.
results.fix: Name the company goal this serves, the research behind it, and the two competitors users already compare you to (Granola, Otter) with where you'll differ.
Strip the stock phrases ('seamlessly', 'revolutionize', 'unprecedented') and rewrite in the voice of your team's best past PRD.
Add a 'Why now' paragraph: what changed, how this differentiates, and how it moves acquisition or monetization, with a number.
Pick one metric with a target and a date, e.g. '40% of weekly-active teams open a summary within 24 hours, by end of Q2.'
List the failure cases: crosstalk, a wrong owner on an action item, confidential meetings, a participant who didn't consent to recording. Say what the product does in each.

results.evidence: All knowledge workers who attend meetings.
results.fix: Name one target segment and add a 'Not in v1' list. Translation, sentiment analysis and speaking-time coaching are obvious candidates.

results.evidence: The engineering team will determine the best architecture.
results.fix: Hand this to an engineer cold and write down every question they'd ask, then answer them in the doc.

results.evidence: We will use a state-of-the-art LLM.
We will build an AI-powered meeting assistant
results.fix: Open with a three-sentence summary an exec can repeat: who, what changes for them, and the bet you're making.
Delete any template section you can't fill with something specific. Goals, Risks and Technical Considerations are filler as written.
Link a clickable prototype of the summary view and cut the feature list down to what the prototype can't show.
Add an Assumptions table: each assumption, its evidence today, and how you'll test it (e.g. 'Users trust AI-assigned action items: untested, run a 10-team pilot').
Define 'accurate' with 20 real meeting transcripts and the ideal summary and action items for each, plus pass/fail rules (e.g. every action item has the correct owner).

results.evidence: As a user, I want summaries so that I can save time.
results.fix: Rewrite each requirement as something checkable: 'Summary lists every decision stated in the meeting; tested against the 20-transcript set.'
Define 'engagement', 'adoption' and 'action item' precisely, including the event that counts each one.

questions: Which user did you watch struggle with this, and what did they do instead?
If you could ship only one of the nine features, which one, and what would make you kill it?
How will you know a summary is good before customers tell you it isn't?
